Ashley N. Bulseco, Wenzhuo Yang, Julie A. Huber, and Joseph J. Vallino. (2026). Growth characteristics of natural microbial populations are skewed toward bacteria with low specific growth rates. Microbiology Spectrum, 14(9), e02193-26. DOI HTML


Abstract

ABSTRACT Microbes are often functionally characterized by traits that specify their optimum environmental conditions for growth, such as temperature or pH, as well as upper and lower bounds where growth is possible. While any given microbe will have a narrow environmental window where growth can occur, a diverse community can span a much larger range of conditions where growth is possible by at least some members of the community. One important trait of microbes is maximum specific growth rate, as this trait determines if a microbe can persist in environments with short residence times. In this study, we conducted a chemostat experiment with natural microbial communities and manipulated dilution rate to test how it would act as a selective force controlling community dynamics and microbial diversity. Using both the experimental chemostats, as well as trait-based modeling, we examined how the composition of a microbial community collected from a coastal meromictic pond changed as dilution rate increased from 0.1 to 10 day−1. We compared experimental results from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequences to the output from two different simulations of the trait-based model, one in which maximum specific growth rate was initially evenly distributed across the community, and another where maximum specific growth rate traits were pulled from a beta probability distribution that was skewed toward low specific growth rates. Experimental results matched the simulation where the initial natural population was dominated by slow-growing microbes, highlighting the importance of initial trait distributions in modeling community response to environmental changes.IMPORTANCE All living organisms are constrained by environmental boundaries that govern where growth is possible, such as minimum and maximum temperatures or pH. An organism’s maximum specific growth rate places a lower bound on the residence or turnover time where an organism can persist without being removed from the system. While there are laboratory constraints on the maximum specific growth rate of culturable microorganisms, such as Escherichia or Vibrio species, information is lacking on how the maximum specific growth rate trait is distributed in natural microbial communities. This information is critical for understanding how a community will respond to changes in residence time or other environmental perturbations. Using chemostats and trait-based modeling, this study assessed how maximum specific growth rate is distributed in a natural community collected from a coastal, salinity-stratified pond.

title: Camille Kroot
text:
Bio
Camille is a master’s student at the University of New Hampshire. Her thesis project investigates microbial community composition and nitrogen cycling in restored New Hampshire salt marshes, particularly if there are noticeable shifts in community and ecosystem function when comparing restored marshes to degraded and healthy marshes. She has participated and led a variety of field work, incubations, and lab work to gain a deeper understanding of microbial communities in changing environments, and their implications. In the future, Camille hopes to pursue a career that combines research and collaboration with the public to connect people to science.

title: Full Name
text:
Bio
Marley is a PhD student whose research focuses on phytoplankton and bacterial community networks in estuarine and saltmarsh systems. She is interested in understanding how phytoplankton community composition changes in concert with other microbes, and how those changes relate to carbon cycling and other ecosystem functions. Marley is co-advised by Dr. Elizabeth Harvey, and her work focuses on combining molecular techniques and bioinformatics with traditional and imaging flow cytometry. Science communication Instagram: @mgg_plankton

Thanks for visiting this webpage, it’s still under construction, if you want to know more about the lab, please reach out to Ashley Bulseco directly.
A longstanding objective in microbial ecology is to link spatial and temporal distributions of microorganisms to ecosystem function and global biogeochemical cycling. As a microbial and ecosystem ecologist, I apply a combination of controlled laboratory experiments and field-based studies that employ next-generation sequencing, bioinformatics, and biogeochemical rate measurements, ultimately aiming to connect biological mechanisms to ecosystem scale processes using a microbial lens. Primary research goals including understanding changes to microbial diversity, structure, and function of coastal ecosystems in response to human activities, and in turn, using microbiome-informed data as an indication of overall ecosystem health. My research program is designed for extensive intellectual contribution and involvement from both undergraduate and graduate students. If you are interested in joining the lab, please reach out!

title: Hannah Holland-Moritz
text:
Bio
Hannah Holland-Moritz is a consulting bioinformatics specialist in the Bulseco group. She also maintains a research program at Syracuse University where she is a Research Assistant Professor. Her research focuses on integrating microbial traits and eco-evolutionary dynamics into predictive models at the community, landscape, and global scales. By combining microbial community data, molecular tools, and quantitative modeling, she examines how microbial traits and interactions mediate carbon and nutrient cycling in terrestrial and synthetic ecosystems. Her research addresses a wide-range of challenges from predicting which bacteria in fermented foods produce flavor-enhancing metabolites to identifying the microorganisms most likely to contribute to climate change in wetlands and polar regions. In addition to her research, Holland-Moritz is an active and enthusiastic supporter of the science of team science and enjoys training and mentoring students in interdisciplinary leadership, informatics, and data science skills.

title: Erin Mansfield
text:
Bio
Erin is a M.S. student in the lab whose research focuses on characterizing oyster microbiomes in Great Bay, NH. She is studying how changes in farming practices, time of year, and other environmental shifts may impact microbiomes, with a goal of identifying microbial communities that may be associated with higher chances of oyster survival. During her graduate studies and in her future career, she hopes to connect with local communities and stakeholders for collaboration and to share her research.

title: Ashley Bulseco
text:
Bio
Ashley’s research focuses on understanding the microbial response to human-driven disturbances in wetland, estuarine, and marine ecosystems. She is particularly interested in whether shifts in the microbial community translate to changes in ecosystem function, especially in relation to carbon and nitrogen cycling. Ashley’s work often takes a multi-faceted approach to address these questions, applying a range of interdisciplinary techniques that combine field work, controlled laboratory experiments, biogeochemical measurements, sequencing, and bioinformatics. Prior to coming to UNH, she taught Environmental Science and Oceanography at the high school level and will continue to explore her passion for innovative and inclusive pedagogical practices in STEM.
